mainEntity.name: Can an infection in a neighbouring tooth cause a dental implant to fail?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is possible, though not inevitable. If a severe infection spreads to the bone surrounding a dental implant, it can contribute to bone loss that may compromise the implant's stability. This is known as retrograde peri-implantitis. The likelihood depends on the severity of the infection, its proximity to the implant, and how promptly treatment is sought. Early professional assessment gives a strong opportunity to protect the implant. Not all infections near implants will lead to implant failure, but the situation always warrants clinical evaluation.

mainEntity.name: What is peri-implantitis, and is it related to neighbouring tooth infections?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implantitis is a condition in which the gum and bone around a dental implant become inflamed and begin to break down, often due to bacterial infection. It is most commonly caused by plaque accumulation on the implant surface, but it can also develop when infection from a neighbouring tooth spreads to the surrounding bone — a form sometimes called retrograde peri-implantitis. Symptoms can include swelling, bleeding around the implant, and discomfort. A dental professional can distinguish between different causes and recommend appropriate management.

mainEntity.name: How quickly can a tooth infection spread to an implant area?

acceptedAnswer.text: The rate at which a dental infection spreads varies depending on several factors, including the type of infection (pulpal or periodontal), the patient's immune response, the density of the surrounding bone, and how close the infected tooth is to the implant. Some infections develop and spread over weeks or months; others may progress more rapidly. This is why dental infections should not be left untreated, particularly in patients with dental implants. Regular monitoring through dental check-ups can help detect problems before they escalate.

mainEntity.name: Is pain around a dental implant always a sign of infection from a neighbouring tooth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Discomfort around a dental implant can have several causes, including peri-implantitis from plaque accumulation on the implant itself, overloading of the implant, problems with the crown or restoration, or issues with the bite. Pain from a neighbouring tooth may also radiate and feel as though it originates from the implant area. A clinical examination, potentially with X-rays, is needed to identify the actual source of discomfort. It is always worth having persistent implant-area pain assessed by a dental professional.

mainEntity.name: Can root canal treatment on a tooth next to an implant protect the implant?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the infection is limited to the pulp of the neighbouring tooth, root canal treatment performed in a timely and effective manner may help prevent the spread of infection to the surrounding bone, which in turn may reduce the risk of the implant being affected. However, the success of this approach depends on the extent of the infection at the time of treatment, the quality of the procedure, and the overall condition of the bone. Treatment suitability must always be assessed on an individual basis by a qualified dental professional.

mainEntity.name: How often should implant patients have dental check-ups?

acceptedAnswer.text: The frequency of dental check-ups for implant patients is typically determined by the dental team based on individual circumstances, including overall oral health, medical history, and the presence of any risk factors such as a history of gum disease. Many dental professionals recommend six-monthly check-ups and hygiene appointments for implant patients, though some individuals may benefit from more frequent monitoring. These appointments allow the implant and surrounding tissues to be assessed regularly, helping to identify any changes at an early stage.
